The Earth’s energy imbalance (EEI) that develops at the top of the atmosphere is accommodated by gains or losses of energy in Earth’s heat reservoirs, leading to temperature and sea level change.

The global ocean has stored about 90% of the EEI from anthropogenic forcing, but the attribution of past changes of EEI remains largely unknown, thus obscuring our understanding of past climate change.

The global energy budget is defined as Δ Ν = Δ F − Δ R , where Δ Ν is the Earth’s energy imbalance (EEI) equivalent to the change in the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) net radiative flux (watts per square meter), Δ F is the incoming effective radiative forcing (watts per square meter), and Δ R is the Earth’s radiative response (watts per square meter) [=λΔ T , where λ is the climate feedback parameter (watts per square meter per kelvin) and Δ T is the change in surface temperature (kelvins)] ( 1 , 2 ).

Due to energy conservation, EEI must be equal to the rate of energy gain or loss from the Earth’s heat reservoirs (atmosphere, cryosphere, land, and ocean), with attendant changes in the global energy inventory that lag the forcing because of the thermal inertia of the climate system and thus provide an important constraint on equilibrium climate sensitivity ( 1 , 3 , 4 ).

Due to energy conservation, EEI must be equal to the rate of energy gain or loss from the Earth’s heat reservoirs (atmosphere, cryosphere, land, and ocean), with attendant changes in the global energy inventory that lag the forcing because of the thermal inertia of the climate system and thus provide an important constraint on equilibrium climate sensitivity ( 1 , 3 , 4 ).

The current global energy budget is derived from satellite radiometers that measure the TOA net radiative flux and from measurements of ocean, atmosphere, and land heat content and ice melting that document changes in the global energy inventory in response to increasing EEI.

Based on reconstructions of changes of mean ocean temperature (ΔMOT) and ice sheet volume, one study ( 7 ) found a positive EEI associated with nearly equivalent energy gains from ocean warming and land-ice melting during Termination I [TI; 21 to 10 thousand years ago (ka)].

Notably, they also identified two peaks in EEI that correspond to strong reductions of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) and millennial-scale ΔMOT variability during Heinrich Stadial 1 (HS1; ∼18 to 14.7 ka) and the Younger Dryas (YD; ∼12.9 to 11.7 ka).

Our reconstructed peaks in EEI ocean represent a two-stage pattern that begins with an emerging stage of a positive EEI ocean peak followed by a diminishing EEI ocean stage during Heinrich stadials ( Fig.
This two-stage EEI response is simulated in a state-of-the-art climate model in iTRACE ( 17 ).

From the oceanic perspective, the increased MOT or initial buildup of positive EEI is caused by the strong meltwater flux over the northern North Atlantic, which weakens deep convection and the associated convective mixing of upward heat flux from the deep ocean to the surface, leading to a subsurface warming (and surface cooling) and, in turn, increased MOT there ( 32 ).
The resulting weakening of the AMOC also reduces the northward oceanic heat transport, accumulating heat and increasing MOT in the tropical and South Atlantic throughout the ocean depth.

In contrast, the current EEI is from anthropogenic forcing ( 3 , 6 ) with ongoing storage of excess energy being partitioned largely (∼90%) in the global ocean.

We calculated uncertainty by converting the ΔMOT uncertainty to energy by using the ∆ E ocean equation ∆ E ice = ( ∆ SL × A ocean × ρ fw × L fw ) × 1.10 where ∆ SL is the change in global sea level ( 11 ), A ocean is the modern ocean area (361.84 × 10 6 km 2 ) ( 47 ), ρ fw is the density of freshwater (1 g/cm 3 ), and L fw is the latent heat of fusion of freshwater (334,000 J/kg).

We calculate uncertainty by converting the global sea level uncertainty ( 11 ) to energy using the same ∆ E ice equation ∆ E atm = ∆ T × m atm × cp atm where ∆ T is global mean air temperature change (°C) ( 30 ), m atm is the mass of Earth’s atmosphere (5.14 × 10 18 kg) ( 48 ), and cp atm (1005 J/kg °C) is the specific heat of the atmosphere.
We calculate uncertainty by converting global temperature uncertainty ( 30 ) to energy using the ∆ E atm equation.
The uncertainty on ΔE global was calculated as the square root of the sum of squares of the uncertainties of Δ E ocean , Δ E ice , and Δ E atm .

We derived the energy imbalance associated with the rates of Δ E ocean , Δ E ice , Δ E atm , and Δ E global (EEI ocean, EEI ice , EEI atm , and EEI, respectively) using the following equation ( 7 , 9 ) EEI = ( ∂ ∆ E ∂ t × 1 A Earth ) where ∂ ∆ E is the change in energy over time ( ∂ t ) in seconds associated with our age resolution (1.578 × 10 10 s in 500 years) and A Earth is the area of the Earth (5.1 × 10 14 m 2 ).

iTRACE simulation iTRACE is a state-of-the-art transient global climate and water isotope simulation of the last deglaciation, performed using iCESM1 ( 17 ).

Four forcing factors—continental ice sheets (ICE), orbital-induced solar insolation (ORB), greenhouse gas concentrations (GHG), and meltwater fluxes (MWF)—were applied additively to simulate deglacial climate evolution since the LGM (20 ka).

The continental ice sheet topography was updated every 1000 years according to the ICE-6G reconstruction ( 55 ), while greenhouse gas concentrations (CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O) were prescribed based on ice-core records ( 56 ).
Because ice sheets were prescribed in the simulation, the global ocean was the only major heat reservoir, that is, EEI ocean ≈ EEI.
